e.etymology: A spelling of Madison, an English surname meaning son of Maud, a medieval form of Matilda. Madison became a girl's name after the mermaid Madison in the 1984 film Splash.
A form of Quentin and the usual spelling in Dutch, from Latin Quintinus, a derivative of quintus, fifth. St. Quentin was a 3rd-century martyr in Gaul.
The Hebrew form of Bathsheba, from bat, daughter, and sheva, which means both oath and seven. In the Bible she is the wife of King David and the mother of Solomon.
A modern American name, a C spelling of Kaliyah, which was built on Aaliyah with a new first letter. It also extends the nickname Cali.
A modern American name that joins Bay to the -len ending of Jalen and Kaylen, in the same family as Baylor and Bailey.
A spelling of Harley, an English place name and surname from Old English hara, hare, and leah, clearing.

assoc.t: Harley Quinn of DC Comics (as Harley)

e.etymology: The French form of Sebastian, from Latin Sebastianus, a man from Sebaste, a city named with the Greek word sebastos, venerable. St. Sebastian was a Roman martyr of the 3rd century.
A modern American name with no settled origin. It sounds like Cree, the name of a Native people of Canada and the northern US, and matches the Kree, an alien race in Marvel comics and films.

assoc.t: the Kree, alien empire in Marvel's Captain Marvel
Cree, a Native people of Canada (sounds the same)

e.etymology: In the US a modern name built on Kai, alongside Makai and Zakai. Akai is also the Japanese adjective for red and a Japanese surname.

assoc.t: Akai, maker of MPC drum machines and audio gear

e.etymology: The Russian form of Greek Niketas, victor, from nike, victory; in Russia it is a man's name. English and French speakers took it up for girls, helped by Elton John's 1985 song Nikita.
namesakes: Nikita Khrushchev (Soviet leader during the Cuban Missile Crisis)

assoc.t: Nikita, the assassin of La Femme Nikita and its TV series

e.etymology: A spelling of Jayden, coined in the US in the late 20th century by putting J in front of the sound of Aidan, Braden and Hayden. It has been used for both boys and girls from the start.
From Old High German liut, people, and bald, bold. The Leo- spelling comes from association with Latin leo, lion. It was a name of Austrian emperors and Belgian kings.
namesakes: Leopold Bloom (hero of James Joyce's Ulysses)
Leopold II (Belgian king notorious for his brutal rule of the Congo)

assoc.t: Leopold and Loeb, 1924 Chicago murder case

e.etymology: A spelling of Lilian that shows its parts as Lily and Ann. Lilian dates from the 1500s, perhaps first as a pet form of Elizabeth, and is linked to Latin lilium, lily.
From the English surname Atlee or Attlee, Middle English atte lee, for someone who lived at the clearing. As a first name it follows Hadley, Oakley and Atlas.
A recent blend of Everly and Evelyn. Everly is an English place-name surname, and Evelyn goes back to the Norman women's name Aveline.
A spelling of Sky, the English word, which comes from Old Norse sky, cloud. This spelling is known from actress Skai Jackson.
namesakes: Skai Jackson (Disney Channel actress in Jessie)

e.etymology: A spelling of Alani, which matches the Hawaiian word alani, orange tree. It is also heard as a form of Alana or Alanna.

e.meaning: rule, pattern, if taken from Latin norma
e.etymology: Made known by Bellini's 1831 opera Norma, about a Druid priestess. It is often explained as Latin norma, rule or pattern, and has also been used as a feminine of Norman.
namesakes: Norma Jeane Mortenson (birth name of Marilyn Monroe)
Norma Rae (union organizer played by Sally Field in the 1979 film)
Norma Desmond (faded silent-film star in Sunset Boulevard)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jasmine, the fragrant flower, whose name came into English through French and Arabic from Persian yasamin.

assoc.t: Princess Jasmine of Disney's Aladdin (as Jasmine)

e.etymology: From Old Irish Ciaran, from ciar, black or dark, with the diminutive ending -an. Early Irish saints made it popular, among them the founder of the monastery of Clonmacnoise. Kieran is the English spelling.
namesakes: Ciaran Hinds (Irish actor in Belfast and Game of Thrones)
e.note: Americans who do not know Irish spelling often read the C as an S, so expect to explain it.

e.etymology: The Hebrew word for beloved, the feminine of ahuv, from the root for love. In the US it is used mostly in Orthodox Jewish families.
A form of Analia, the Spanish combination of Ana and Lia, written with the double n of Anna.

A spelling of Jasiel or Jaasiel, a minor Old Testament name borne by one of King David's warriors, from Hebrew for God makes. It is used mostly in Spanish-speaking families, alongside Jaziel and Yadiel.

e.meaning: on the moon in Turkish; also a form of Aida
e.etymology: In Turkish, ay, moon, with the ending -da, on or in. Ayda also serves as a spelling of Aida, known from Verdi's opera and as an Arabic name meaning returning.
A modern name that writes Bowden or Boden with Beau, French for handsome, in front of the -den ending of Jayden and Hayden. Bowden is an English surname.
A French pet form of Francoise (Frances), from Late Latin Franciscus, Frenchman or Frank. It was most popular in the US in the 1940s.
namesakes: Francine Smith (the mother on American Dad!)
Francine Frensky (Arthur's friend on the PBS series Arthur)

assoc.t: Hurricane Francine, which struck Louisiana in 2024

e.etymology: A short form of Montgomery, a Norman place name meaning Gomeric's hill, and of Montague, pointed hill.
namesakes: Monty Hall (host of Let's Make a Deal)

assoc.t: the full monty, meaning the whole thing

e.meaning: manly, as a form of Drew from Andrew
e.etymology: A spelling of Drew, the short form of Andrew, from Greek andreios, manly. Drue was also an old English form of the Norman name Drogo.
A modern American coinage that puts the Ty- of Tyler and Tyson with the -len ending of Jalen and Kylen. It has no meaning of its own.
e.note: Spelled like the start of Tylenol, the pain reliever, so expect that as a nickname or joke.

e.etymology: A spelling of Aliza, from Hebrew aliza, joyful or cheerful.
A modern American coinage that joins the Ky- of Kyler and Kyson to zen. It also echoes kaizen, the Japanese word for continuous improvement, which is used as a name in the spelling Kaizen.
A spelling of Cameron, the Scottish clan surname from Gaelic cam, crooked, and sron, nose.
namesakes: Cam'ron (Harlem rapper behind Hey Ma and Oh Boy)
